name: Prudentius of Troyes
knownFor: Spanish-born bishop of Troyes who kept the annals now called the Annals of Saint-Bertin until his death in 861. He took the side of double predestination against Hincmar of Reims.
dates: Kept the annals from 835, after a first writer who stopped in the middle of that year, G. H. Pertz says. Died in 861, by Hincmar's entry for that year. At councils at Paris in 846 and at Soissons in 853, says Nicolás Antonio, a Spanish scholar writing after 1650. No held source gives his birth
place: Born in Hesperia and brought to the Celts, by his own verses for a Gospel book; Nicolás Antonio takes Hesperia to be Spain. Bishop of Troyes

keyWorks.title: Annals of Saint-Bertin, from the 830s to 861
keyWorks.about: the annals of the deeds of the Frankish kings, which Hincmar says Prudentius composed and the king held. Georg Waitz says some have held them to be official annals and others have doubted it

keyWorks.title: On Predestination, against John Scotus
keyWorks.about: his answer to nineteen chapters taken from the book of John Scotus Eriugena, written at the request of Wenilo, archbishop of Sens

keyWorks.title: Letter to Hincmar and Pardulus
keyWorks.about: a letter on predestination to Hincmar of Reims and Pardulus of Laon, which Antonio dates to 849

traces: Hincmar took over the annals after Prudentius's death, G. H. Pertz says. Hincmar carried them on almost to the end of his own life, Georg Waitz says.

His entry under 859, that Pope Nicholas the First had confirmed a double predestination, made Hincmar write to Egilo of Sens. Hincmar asked that the pope be told, so that no scandal should come to the church.
Antonio says he sent a letter, his Tractoria, to the synod of Sens. In it he held that Aeneas, chosen bishop of Paris, must sign four statements first.
remembered: Hincmar calls him learned, but says he turned in bitterness into a fierce defender of Gottschalk's heresy. Hincmar was his opponent in the predestination quarrel.
Nicolás Antonio calls the annal on him a slander. He gives it to an unnamed annalist on Hincmar's side, and says Prudentius never opposed Gottschalk.

A note in a manuscript of his treatise, printed in Patrologia Latina 115, warns that he did not think rightly on some teachings. Nicolaus Camusat of Troyes answers that it came perhaps from someone who could not follow him.
Antonio says the church of Troyes calls him a saint in its lists of bishops.

uncertain: Whether he ever opposed Gottschalk. Hincmar says he first resisted him and then took his side. Antonio says he never opposed him.
Most of what is told of his life comes through Hincmar, his opponent, and the annals. The rest comes through defenders who answered them, such as Nicolás Antonio.

The entry on Gottschalk under 849. G. H. Pertz says learned men judge that Prudentius could not have written it as it stands, and that Hincmar changed it. A note from Bouquet's edition, which Waitz prints, gives the abbé Lebeuf's guess at the first wording.
His name. Hincmar calls him Galindo, surnamed Prudentius. Antonio says a count Galindo of Aragon shows the name is Spanish. He asks what stops Prudentius being of the same family.
